Storytellers do not need to allow this Merit ever, as legendary artifacts are innately and grossly unfair plot devices that will likely dominate any series they occupy.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble, at Storyteller discretion (heavily discouraged by the book's own text); for a raksha this would most plausibly be a unique, story-specific Wyld Artifact, Adjuration, or Behemoth on the scale of the gm-only ishiika row rather than an ordinary purchase from the raksha's own dot-tiered options.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-merit-legendary-artifact. No splat-specific language exists anywhere in this entry; it applies to Fair Folk exactly as written. Cross-referenced against ishiika, this family's own existing example of a one-off, story-specific artifact-tier treasure vastly beyond the normal purchasable options, as the closest raksha-appropriate parallel to the Merit's own Mantle of Brigid / Eye of Autochthon examples.

name: Cache
summary: The character has wealth hidden or legally stored across many locations, for one bonus point per city beyond the character's home; requires a high enough wealth rating to draw on. Reinterpreted for raksha as requiring Gossamer 2+ (which grants an effective Resources 4 in Creation), since Fair Folk do not use the Resources Background at all.
requirements: Gossamer 2+ (gossamer-background), which grants an effective Resources 4 in Creation and therefore satisfies this Merit's prerequisite.
mechanics: The character has wealth hidden or legally stored in many locations, for a cost of one bonus point per city beyond the character's home. The character has full access to the value of her full wealth at any of these locations and their surrounding regions; five points of Cache grant access in any settlement town-sized or larger in a selected direction of Creation (money may take up to a week to arrive from another direction), and every point beyond five extends the domain by another direction.
compatibility: Any raksha with Gossamer 2+; reinterpreted from the original Resources 4+/Salary 2+ prerequisite, since raksha exclude the Resources Background entirely and use Gossamer as their wealth-and-influence Background instead (see gossamer-background, followers-and-resources-excluded-fair-folk).
notes: JUDGMENT CALL / REINTERPRETATION: this Merit's prerequisite (Resources 4+ or Salary 2+) does not exist verbatim for Fair Folk, since raksha exclude the Resources Background entirely (see followers-and-resources-excluded-fair-folk) in favor of Gossamer. Gossamer's own dot table (gossamer-background) explicitly equates 2 dots of Gossamer to 'effective Resources 4' in Creation, which was used here as the direct, well-grounded substitute prerequisite rather than excluding the Merit outright.

name: Alternative Divination
summary: Crude divination through methods other than astrology (tea leaves, entrails, palm-reading, crystal-gazing, etc.); each purchase grants knowledge of one ritual, capped by the character's Occult rating. Raksha with an Occult rating (a Caste Ability for Diplomats, and purchasable by any raksha) may take this exactly as written.
requirements: An Occult rating; may not be purchased more times than the character's Occult rating.
mechanics: Characters with this Merit can crudely divine the workings of fate through methods other than astrology -- tea leaves, entrails, palm-reading, crystal-gazing, drug-induced trance verses, and the like. Rolls and effectiveness match conventional astrology (see Exalted, p. 251); any divination ritual takes at least one scene, with quicker or less complicated methods suffering an increased difficulty and elaborate, well-described rituals benefiting from a stunt bonus. Each purchase grants knowledge of one effective ritual.
compatibility: Any raksha with an Occult rating, common or noble; the Sidereal-specific two-rituals-per-purchase upgrade does not extend to Fair Folk.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-merit-alternative-divination, which documents a Sidereal-specific two-rituals-per-purchase upgrade. That upgrade is named for a different splat and does not extend to Fair Folk, but the base Merit carries no eligibility restriction, and Occult is a Diplomat Caste Ability (see diplomat-caste), so it applies to Fair Folk at the ordinary cost.

name: Priest
summary: Recognized priest of a deity/religion; the 1-pt. version is automatically and freely granted to a handful of specific Exalted castes as an innate part of their Exaltation. Raksha have no such innate free grant, since no Fair Folk caste is tied to any deity's priesthood, but any raksha may purchase either version normally -- most plausibly as a cleric of the Church of Balor, the raksha nobility's own faith, already noted as a character-creation concept prompt.
mechanics: The character is a recognized priest of a particular deity or religion. Apart from lowering the difficulty of prayers directed at the appropriate spirit (see Exalted, p. 335), the one-point version has no defined rules effects, though Storytellers may award symbolic dream messages or omens. The seven-point high-priest version signifies far greater favor, granting portentous dreams and the ability to petition the patron for miracles via a standard prayer roll (spending a Willpower point for an automatic success, or channeling an appropriate Virtue); successes may restore Essence or spent Willpower, exorcise a possessing spirit, or heal a dying character, at the Storyteller's discretion. Spirits can perceive a distinctive mark on characters with this Merit, its design and placement dependent on the patron.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble, at the full, undiscounted cost -- no Fair Folk caste receives an innate free version the way certain Exalted castes do, since Diplomat/Entertainer/Warrior/Worker are not religious castes. A raksha priest of the Church of Balor (see fair-folk-creation-overview-noble) is the most thematically direct fit.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-merit-priest, which documents an innate free grant for specific Exalted castes (including No Moon Caste Lunars). Fair Folk's four base castes (Diplomat/Entertainer/Warrior/Worker) are not religious castes, so no innate grant transfers; instead, this row leans on fair-folk-creation-overview-noble's own mention of the Church of Balor as an in-fiction faith a raksha noble might already belong to, making the ordinary purchased version of this Merit a natural fit for Fair Folk at full cost.

name: Destiny
summary: Represents an auspicious fate written in the stars, scaling from a lifetime of good health (1 pt.) up to founding a lasting noble dynasty or transforming an era (5 pts.). The book's cap only restricts Celestial and Abyssal/Infernal Exalted, whose free will overrides most of their pre-Exaltation Destiny; raksha are not Exalted at all and were never assigned any Destiny by the Loom of Fate in the first place, so they take the uncapped, mortal-facing 1-5 pt. range, flagged here as a genuine conceptual tension worth a Storyteller's attention.
mechanics: A character with Destiny lives most auspiciously, his fate written large in the stars. A one-point destiny may be a long and uneventful life of good health; two points, financial prosperity or many offspring; three points, the destinies of merchant princes or kings of small nations; four points, a hero whose deeds live on for generations, or the founder of a lasting dynasty; five points, the mightiest sorcerers and emperors whose exploits transform their era. Destiny need not be kind to those who bear it -- greatness may be rooted in tyranny or culminate in tragedy. Storytellers should ensure coincidence protects those with a powerful fate until it finds fruition. Players may request a particular destiny or leave the specifics to the Storyteller.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble, at the full 1-5 pt. range; the book's cap on retained Destiny applies only to Celestial and Abyssal/Infernal Exalted whose Exaltation overrides a pre-existing mortal fate, a process raksha never undergo.
notes: JUDGMENT CALL: the book's companion 'Destiny and Exaltation' sidebar caps Celestial/Abyssal/Infernal Exalted at 1-2 points of retained Destiny because their free will at Exaltation overrides a pre-existing mortal Destiny rating. Raksha are not Exalted and are not born as mortals whose Destiny gets consumed by an Exaltation event, so that specific cap does not textually apply; this row takes the full 1-5 pt. mortal-facing range. Flagged as a genuine conceptual tension worth Storyteller attention: raksha are beings of the Wyld, canonically outside the Loom of Fate that this Merit represents, so a Storyteller may reasonably rule that Destiny (and, likewise, pg-flaw-dark-fate and pg-flaw-unbidden-oracle below) apply only to a raksha who has spent significant time settled within Creation, if at all -- the Players Guide text itself gives no such restriction, so this row is included as selectable rather than excluded by inference.

name: Lucky
summary: Grants a luck pool the player may spend to reroll dice or shift random events. Raksha use the base 1-5 pt. formula, since the alternate luck-pool formula and price cap are named for Sidereal Exalted specifically.
mechanics: A character with this Merit is blessed with an unlikely preponderance of fortune. Lucky characters receive a luck pool equal to the points invested; players may spend points of luck to repeat any roll (even a botch, barring certain curse-based exceptions) at the same difficulty and target number, or to shift a game of chance or other random event (each point spent increases the character's chance of success by 10 percent, per a Storyteller die roll). Characters regain one luck point after a full week without spending any, and refresh the pool fully at the end of each story.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; the Sidereal-specific luck-pool formula and 3-pt. price cap do not extend to Fair Folk.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-merit-lucky, which documents a Sidereal-specific luck-pool formula and price cap. That variant is named for a different splat and does not extend to Fair Folk; raksha use the ordinary 1-5 pt. formula, since the base Merit carries no eligibility restriction. Cross-referenced against pg-merit-destiny, a related but mechanically distinct Trait, per the source text.

name: Signature Style
summary: Combines movement and attitude into a distinctive flair defining the character's legend; functions like an Ability specialty for stunts, granting an extra die that stacks with the stunt-rating die. A purely narrative Merit with no eligibility restriction to adapt.
mechanics: Characters with this Merit combine movement and attitude into a distinctive flair that defines their legend, functioning like an Ability specialty for stunts and providing one extra die in appropriate circumstances; this extra die stacks with the stunt rating but does not alter motes or Willpower returned on success. Characters may purchase this Merit up to three times, but only one Signature Style can benefit the same stunt.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; unmodified from the Players Guide text.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-merit-signature-style. No splat-specific language exists anywhere in this entry; it applies to Fair Folk exactly as written, and complements this family's own Wyld Stunts and Wyld Bonuses mechanic well.

name: Prescient Dreamer
summary: Regular prophetic dreams of possible futures, deciphered with Intelligence + Occult. Raksha pay the ordinary cost, since the discounted price is named for Sidereal Exalted specifically.
mechanics: A character with this Merit regularly dreams of what may be, recognizing them as visions even without knowing their meaning. Deriving meaning requires an Intelligence + Occult roll at a difficulty reflecting the event's significance; more successes reveal more clarity. Such dreams come unbidden and follow the whims of fate and the Storyteller. Revealing the dream's content or acting on it interferes with that destiny and decreases its overall probability.
compatibility: Any raksha with an Occult rating, common or noble; the discounted 2-pt. cost is named for Sidereal Exalted specifically and does not extend to Fair Folk.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-merit-prescient-dreamer, which documents a Sidereal-specific discount tied to Sidereals' fate-based Exaltation. That reasoning does not apply to raksha, who neither Exalt nor administer Fate; raksha purchase this Merit at the ordinary, undiscounted cost.

name: Daredevil
summary: Fortune smiles on the recklessly brave: may reflexively spend one Willpower point to double the rating of a stunt awarded for a Physical action, with a difficulty of 3 or higher. A purely mechanical Merit with no eligibility restriction to adapt.
mechanics: A character with this Merit may reflexively spend one Willpower point to double the rating of stunt dice awarded to a Physical action with a difficulty of 3 or higher, after the Storyteller determines the stunt rating; this does not prevent simultaneous Willpower use for automatic success or checking a Virtue, and does not increase the motes or Willpower returned by a successful stunt. Characters with the Signature Style Merit do not double the extra die awarded by that Trait when both apply.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; unmodified from the Players Guide text (the heroic-mortal discount does not apply to raksha).
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-merit-daredevil. No splat-specific language exists anywhere in this entry beyond a heroic-mortal discount, which does not apply to raksha; it applies to Fair Folk at the ordinary 4-pt. cost.

name: Mute
summary: Cannot speak or make vocal utterance of any sort; players describe actions without speech, using sign language, magic, or shared understanding. Higher tiers add physical/vocal-cord damage. Raksha pay the ordinary cost, since the 1-point discount is named for Exalted generically and Fair Folk are not Exalted.
mechanics: Mute characters may not speak or make vocal utterance of any sort; their players describe actions without verbal communication, relying on writing, magic, or a shared sign language. For three points, this limitation has no physiological basis (the character may have forsaken speech as a taboo or vow, and must buy off the Flaw at normal cost if she breaks her silence). The four-point version involves actual damage to the vocal cords. Characters incapable of speaking above a faint whisper may purchase this Flaw for one point, regardless of cause.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; pays the full, undiscounted cost at every tier, since the 1-point-less discount is stated 'for Exalted' generically and raksha are not Exalted.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-merit-mute (transcribed as a Merit-column id in the Lunar inventory despite being a Physical Flaw, per that book's own layout at the Merits/Flaws chapter boundary). The Exalted discount named in the source text does not extend to Fair Folk; raksha take this Flaw at the ordinary, undiscounted cost.

name: Sterile
summary: Physically incapable of siring or bearing children, whether from accident, illness, or a cruel jest of fate; only worth points for characters who can otherwise enjoy the act of procreation, with a wider point range for the impotent/eunuchs. Raksha take the base 1-2 pt. range, since the higher 3-pt. tier is tied to Realm Dynastic social stigma specifically.
mechanics: The character is physically incapable of siring or bearing children, whether from accident, illness, or a cruel jest of fate. This Flaw is only worth one point for characters who can still engage in and enjoy the act of procreation; characters who are also impotent or eunuchs gain two points from the Flaw.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble, at the base 1-2 pt. range; the higher 3-pt. tier is tied to Realm Dynastic social stigma specifically and would only extend to a Fair Folk-appropriate status-conscious court at Storyteller discretion.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-sterile, which documents a higher 3-pt. tier tied to Realm Dragon-Blooded/Dynast social expectations. That specific social context does not exist for raksha, so this row takes the base 1-2 pt. range, noting the higher tier could still apply at Storyteller discretion for a raksha whose noble court places similar weight on heirs and succession (see birth-background).

name: Unusual Appearance
summary: Hair/eyes of a striking, unnatural color at 1 point, or fully piebald/colorless (albino) skin and hairlessness at 2 points; the appearance must deviate notably from the local norm to qualify. A purely physical Flaw with no eligibility restriction to adapt.
mechanics: For one point, the character has hair and/or eyes of a striking, unnatural color; for two points, the character's skin also exhibits remarkable pigmentation or the colorless white of an albino, or the character has no body hair at all. The appearance must deviate notably from the expected local norm to warrant the Flaw. Those marked by striking colors have a harder time hiding or impersonating others and may suffer discrimination (losing one die from pertinent Stealth, Larceny and Social rolls).
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; applies to whatever Mote-shape or elemental form the character currently wears.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-unusual-appearance. No splat-specific language exists anywhere in this entry; it applies to Fair Folk exactly as written.

name: One Eye
summary: Only a single eye remaining (injury or congenital defect): one-die penalty to Awareness rolls involving distance vision or peripheral vision on the blind side, and increases the difficulty of ranged attacks against the character by one. A purely physical Flaw with no eligibility restriction to adapt.
mechanics: Whether resulting from injury or congenital defect, characters with this Flaw have only a single eye remaining, imposing a one-die penalty to Awareness rolls involving distance vision or peripheral vision on the blind side, and increasing the difficulty of ranged attacks against the character by one.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; unmodified from the Players Guide text.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-one-eye. No splat-specific language exists anywhere in this entry; it applies to Fair Folk exactly as written.

name: Sun-Seared
summary: Uncomfortable in sunlight, suffering horrible sunburns from relatively mild exposure. A purely physical Flaw with no eligibility restriction to adapt; the ghost/Abyssal flavor example for the most extreme tier is setting color, not a mechanical requirement.
mechanics: The character finds sunlight uncomfortable and suffers horrible sunburns from relatively mild exposure. The two-point version imposes -1 on all dice pools in direct sunlight and one die of unsoakable bashing damage per hour of direct exposure; the three-point version increases the penalty to -2 and the damage interval to every 30 minutes; the rare six-point version imposes -3 and damages every minute. Heavy clothing or indirect exposure (overcast skies, shadow-to-shadow movement) doubles the relevant interval.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; the source text's ghost/Abyssal flavor example for the six-point tier is setting color, not an eligibility restriction, so any raksha may take this Flaw at any tier if narratively appropriate.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-sun-seared. Lunar's own notes found the ghost/Abyssal mention to be flavor about typical severity, not an eligibility restriction; it applies to Fair Folk exactly as written.

name: Climate Sensitive
summary: Discomfort and penalties outside the character's accustomed environmental conditions; the point value scales with how common the undesired conditions are to encounter. A purely physical Flaw with no eligibility restriction to adapt.
mechanics: Characters with this Flaw experience discomfort and take ill outside conditions they are accustomed to. For two points, the character responds poorly to one temperature/humidity extreme; for three points, to any environment lacking those conditions; for four points, the defining condition of the character's home region cannot be replicated or transplanted without considerable difficulty. Whenever in an uncomfortable environment, the character adds 1 to the difficulty of all Survival, Endurance and Resistance rolls related to the conditions.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; may be taken to represent discomfort in Creation's climates versus the Wyld's, or vice versa, at Storyteller discretion.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-climate-sensitive. No splat-specific language exists anywhere in this entry; it applies to Fair Folk exactly as written.

name: Amputee
summary: Missing one or more limbs from congenital defect or later injury; scaled by number/type of limbs lost. Raksha take the full mortal-tier cost range, since the reduced range is stated "for Exalted" generically and Fair Folk are not Exalted.
mechanics: The character lacks an arm or a leg (or both), either congenitally or from later injury, or retains the limb only as a useless, paralyzed husk. Characters missing a hand cannot perform two-handed tasks; missing both hands makes fine-dexterity tasks impossible without magic or prosthetics (at a -1 die penalty). Characters missing a leg move at half rate and suffer a -3 penalty to Athletics rolls involving footwork; those missing both legs, or otherwise quadriplegic, may not attempt most physical tasks. The value of this Flaw is two points for a single arm, three for a single arm-and-both-hands combination or similar, five points for the loss of any two limbs, and higher still for quadriplegia.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble, at the full mortal-tier cost; the reduced cost named 'for Exalted' generically does not extend to Fair Folk. A raksha could alternatively represent this via a permanent, Storyteller-approved missing-limb mutation on her Mote if preferred.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-amputee, which documents an Exalted-wide cost reduction. That discount does not extend to Fair Folk; raksha take the full, undiscounted cost range. Lunar's own notes flag this entry's cost text as unusually garbled in the source print; that caveat is preserved here for a future closer read against the rendered page.

name: Dying
summary: A curse, terminal illness, or other fatal condition that will assuredly kill the character without powerful curative magic; loses a dot of Stamina per interval, dying at Stamina 0. A purely physical Flaw with no eligibility restriction to adapt, though Storytellers are advised to be cautious allowing it for powerful supernatural characters.
mechanics: A character with this Flaw suffers a curse, terminal illness, or other fatal condition and will assuredly perish without powerful curative magic. The character loses one dot of Stamina per interval (the length determined by the Flaw's value, shortening from years down to days as the value rises); at Stamina 0, the character dies. This process can always be averted before returning to full heroic effort, but not without truly heroic effort.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; the Storyteller is advised to be more cautious allowing this Flaw for powerful supernatural characters (including noble raksha) absent a strong story reason, exactly as for Exalted.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-dying. The book's caution about allowing this Flaw for powerful characters is advisory rather than a hard exclusion, and applies equally well to a powerful noble raksha as to a Solar or Lunar Exalt.

name: Small
summary: Stands only four and a half feet tall or less, with a reduced effective Strength for weapon/tool size requirements and one fewer -1 health level. A raksha with this Flaw appears proportionally smaller in every shape she assumes via her Assumption-type Charms, since her Mote is a chosen form rather than a fixed body.
mechanics: A character with this Flaw stands only four and a half feet tall or less, reducing her effective Strength by one dot for meeting the minimum requirements of weapons and large tools, and costing her one -1 health level. In addition to representing children, short adults, or pygmy races, this Flaw can portray extremely gaunt and frail characters of normal height, especially alongside low Stamina.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; the size reduction persists across any shape assumed via Assumption-type Charms.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-small, which documents this Flaw's size reduction carrying into every Lunar shapechanged form (mirroring the Large Size Merit's Lunar clause). Fair Folk have no Prey's Skin Disguise equivalent, but the underlying logic transfers exactly as it did for pg-merit-large-size: a raksha has no true form, only Motes and elemental shapes assumed through the universal Assumption-type Charm tree (see assumption-of-elemental-shape), so this Flaw's size reduction is reinterpreted as persisting across whatever shape she currently wears.

name: Disfigured
summary: Wretched physical deformity, from concealable scarring/pockmarks (3-pt., Appearance capped at 1) to monstrous full-body horror (4-pt., Appearance 0, automatic social revulsion). The source text's Lunar-Tell flavor example was reinterpreted for a raksha whose Mote never quite settles into a stable, attractive shape -- a fittingly Wyld-flavored justification in its own right.
mechanics: For three points, the character bears pitted pockmarks, gross birth defects, heavy scarring, useless protrusions of Wyld-warped flesh, or something stranger still, capping Appearance at 1 and losing one die from other Social pools where the deformity could prove a hindrance; heavy clothing or masks can conceal it. The four-point version is truly monstrous -- full-body scarring, gaping abscesses, hideous Wyld-mutation, or worse -- fixing Appearance at 0 (unimprovable) and automatically failing Appearance-based rolls; all but the most tolerant (Compassion 4+) respond with a two-die Social penalty from utter revulsion.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; a raksha's own Wyld-warped, imperfectly stabilized Mote is at least as fitting a source for this Flaw as any Creation-born character's mutation or curse.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-disfigured, whose own worked example is 'a Lunar with a hideous Tell' (a mechanic Fair Folk lack) and a separate Abyssal rotted-visage cross-reference (not relevant to Fair Folk). Both flavor examples were dropped in favor of noting that a raksha's own unstable, Wyld-warped Mote-shape is a natural in-fiction source for this Flaw without needing either borrowed mechanic.

name: Slow Healing
summary: Recovers from injury at half the normal (mortal) rate. Raksha take the base mortal-tier effect rather than the milder Exalted variant, since Fair Folk's own core book grants no superior baseline healing rate to offset against -- their sub-real Wyld-damage immunity (innate-powers-wyld-immunity) is an unrelated mechanic.
mechanics: Characters with this Flaw recover from injury at half their normal rate. Most such characters do not live long in the brutal Age of Sorrows.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble, at the base mortal-tier effect; the milder version described 'for Exalted' (normal mortal healing rate rather than half-mortal) does not extend to Fair Folk, since raksha have no stated baseline healing rate faster than a mortal's to begin with.
notes: JUDGMENT CALL: Lunar's row documents a distinct, milder Exalted variant (mortal rate instead of half-mortal rate) rather than a cost discount. Fair Folk's core book grants raksha no faster-than-mortal baseline healing rate to soften in the first place -- innate-powers-wyld-immunity only protects against sub-real Wyld damage, an unrelated mechanic -- so this Flaw was left at its full, unmodified mortal-tier severity for Fair Folk rather than importing the Exalted variant.

name: Weak Immune System
summary: Harder time fighting off illness. Raksha take the base mortal-tier cost and effect, since the milder Exalted variant and reduced cost are stated "for Exalted" generically and Fair Folk are not Exalted.
mechanics: Characters with this Flaw have a harder time fighting off illness, adding 2 to the difficulty of all Endurance and Resistance rolls to resist disease and infection.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble, at the base mortal-tier cost and effect; the reduced 3-pt. cost and milder halved-dice-pool variant are stated 'for Exalted' generically and do not extend to Fair Folk.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-weak-immune-system, which documents an Exalted-wide discount and milder mechanical variant. That variant does not extend to Fair Folk; raksha take the full mortal-tier cost and severity.

name: Diminished Attributes
summary: Weaker, slower, less healthy (or, in the Mental/Social variants, less bright/uncouth) bodies than normal adults; grants three points per Physical Attribute dot forfeited during character creation. A purely physical/mental/social Flaw with no eligibility restriction to adapt.
mechanics: Characters with this Flaw have weaker, slower, or less healthy bodies than normal adults, receiving three points for every Physical Attribute dot forfeited during character creation. Characters cannot forfeit the free dot received in each Attribute, and may not spend bonus points to purchase Physical Attributes if taking this Flaw. Alternate versions apply to Mental and Social Attributes.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; a noble raksha forfeits from her starting 3-dot-per-Attribute baseline, a common raksha from her 0-dot baseline (see fair-folk-creation-overview-noble / -common).
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-diminished-attributes. No splat-specific language exists anywhere in this entry; it applies to Fair Folk exactly as written, forfeiting from whichever starting Attribute baseline (noble or common) the character uses.

name: Diminished Sense
summary: Partial or total loss of a sense. Raksha take the base mortal-tier value, since the reduced point value and one-sense-loss cap are stated "for Exalted" generically and Fair Folk are not Exalted.
mechanics: The character suffers partial or total loss of a sense, adding 1 to the difficulty of Awareness rolls (and other Storyteller-determined rolls) based on the dulled sense for partial loss. Total loss of a sense causes automatic failure of any roll exclusively dependent on it, and adds 1 to 3 to rolls requiring a conjunction of the missing sense with others. Partial loss is normally worth two or three bonus points depending on the sense; total loss ranges from three points (smell/taste) to six points (blindness).
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble, at the base mortal-tier value; the reduced per-sense value and one-Diminished-Sense-total cap are stated 'for Exalted' generically and do not extend to Fair Folk.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-diminished-sense, which documents an Exalted-wide point reduction and a one-sense-loss cap. Neither extends to Fair Folk; raksha take this Flaw at its full mortal-tier value with no stacking cap beyond ordinary Storyteller discretion.

name: Derangement
summary: The curse of madness, drawing from the Exalted core rulebook's derangement list or the book's own suggested forms (Depression, Glossolalia, Hysteria, Sadism); suppressible for a scene with a Willpower point but only curable by magic or lengthy counseling. A purely mental Flaw with no eligibility restriction to adapt.
mechanics: A character with this Flaw suffers the curse of madness, drawn from the derangement list on page 281 of Exalted or the book's own suggested forms (Depression, Glossolalia, Hysteria, Sadism, each mirroring a specific Virtue Flaw). The worst effects can be suppressed for a scene for one Willpower point, but only magic or lengthy counseling can actually cure a derangement; the character loses at least two dice from most Social pools with characters who do not share the madness. Characters receive three points for their first derangement and one point for each subsequent form.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; a raksha's derangement could plausibly stem from a Bedlam episode gone especially poorly, at Storyteller discretion, though the Flaw itself is independent of Bedlam.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-derangement. No splat-specific language exists anywhere in this entry; it applies to Fair Folk exactly as written. Cross-referenced against bedlam-overview only as an optional in-fiction origin story, since a raksha's Bedlam is otherwise a distinct, separately-tracked mechanic from this Flaw.

name: Amnesia
summary: Large gaps in the character's memory, from a single missing life event (1 pt.) up to recurring amnesia that prevents remembering anything prior to the last sleep (5 pts.). Raksha take the general mortal-facing 1/2/5-pt. scale only; the Celestial-Exalted-specific 1-pt. variant tied to remembering nothing of prior incarnations does not apply, since raksha do not reincarnate the way Solar/Lunar/Sidereal Essence does.
mechanics: Characters with this Flaw suffer large gaps in memory. For one point, the character is missing a notable section of life or a crucial event; for two points, everything before a major turning point; for five points, the amnesia is recurring, preventing the character from remembering anything prior to waking from her last sleep (though her Traits and capabilities remain intact, unremembered). Recurring amnesia also prevents learning or advancing Abilities unless the character can stay awake or keep a thorough journal.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble, at the general 1/2/5-pt. scale; the additional Celestial-Exalted-specific 1-pt. use case (remembering nothing of past incarnations) does not apply, since Fair Folk have no reincarnating-Essence mechanic for it to key off of.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-amnesia, which adds a Celestial-Exalted-specific 1-pt. option (complementing the excluded Past Lives Merit, pg-merit-past-lives, which was not derived for Fair Folk). That specific option was dropped here since raksha have no equivalent reincarnation mechanic, but the general mortal-facing 1/2/5-pt. amnesia scale applies to Fair Folk unmodified.

name: Superstition
summary: A wrong or fanatical idea about something important, treated by the character as sincere fact; scales from a simple personal inconvenience (1 pt.) to a belief that seriously harms others if acted upon (3 pts.). A purely mental Flaw with no eligibility restriction to adapt.
mechanics: Characters with this Flaw hold a wrong or fanatical idea about something important, once perhaps rooted in fact but no longer. For one point, the custom is simply inconvenient; for two points, it is dangerous to the character or believers; for three points, it involves harm to others. Characters who discover and accept the falsehood of their superstitions must buy off this Flaw with experience; characters receive one less point if the game takes place mostly where the belief is commonly held.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; unmodified from the Players Guide text.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-superstition. No splat-specific language exists anywhere in this entry; it applies to Fair Folk exactly as written, and could equally represent a raksha's mistaken belief about Creation, cold-wrought iron, or another raksha court's customs.

name: Vice
summary: A moral weakness, sin, or failing that tempts the character above all others; when relevant, the character loses two dice from the affected Virtue for every point invested and may indulge in it over better judgment. Reinterpreted for raksha as interacting with Bedlam (this splat's Limit-Trait analog) rather than the Lunar-specific Great Curse, since raksha have no Great Curse at all.
mechanics: A character with this Flaw suffers a particular sin or failing that tempts him above all others -- a warrior of great Valor harboring a secret fear, an ascetic of great Temperance falling to carnal desire, deep Compassion masking cruelty or bigotry. In situations relevant to the sinful condition, the character loses two dice from the affected Virtue for every point invested, potentially reducing the pool to zero and forcing automatic indulgence over better judgment. Characters may not have more than one Vice; those with deeper moral deficiencies are Callous instead (see pg-flaw-callous). This Flaw may not alter or ameliorate a raksha's Bedlam, and Storytellers should ban any Vice that obviously attempts to circumvent that restriction.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; may not alter or ameliorate Bedlam (see bedlam-overview, virtue-bedlam-curses), this splat's Limit-Trait analog, exactly as the original text bars it from altering the Great Curse for Solars/Lunars.
notes: REINTERPRETATION: Lunar's row cross-references 'the-great-curse,' Lunars' own Limit-Trait analog, which this Flaw may not alter or ameliorate. Fair Folk have no Great Curse; their structurally closest equivalent is Bedlam (see bedlam-overview, virtue-bedlam-curses), a Virtue-channel-based break mechanic. The restriction was redirected there rather than dropped, preserving the original entry's intent (a Vice cannot be used to weaken or bypass a character's core psychological-break mechanic).

name: Addiction
summary: An addiction to some substance, scaling 1-3 points by legality/danger/expense, plus modifiers for how the habit strains the character's finances or consumes her life. Raksha take the base rating (no Exalted discount, since Fair Folk are not Exalted); the source's Wyld-addiction cross-reference to Lunars' own book was redirected to this family's own Cup Grace Addiction Charms, a closer thematic fit for a being of the Wyld.
mechanics: Characters with this Flaw suffer an addiction to some substance, without which they suffer withdrawal. One point covers a relatively easy, legal, inexpensive and reasonably safe substance (alcohol, qat, marijuana); two points, a rarer or more debilitating substance (opium, rasp spider venom); three points, an expensive and/or dangerous substance (rock cocaine, heroin, bright morning). Add one to the value if the character's wealth cannot support regular use, or two if she cannot afford a single dose or the addiction controls her entire life. Actual withdrawal effects depend on the substance and Storyteller discretion.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble, at the base (non-Exalted) rating; a raksha's addiction could as easily be to feeding itself as to any mortal substance -- see this family's own Cup Grace Addiction Charms (shiftless-untamed-beauty, maddening-summons, whispers-behind-the-eyes) for a raksha-appropriate framing of compulsive craving.
notes: REINTERPRETATION: Lunar's row documents both an Exalted-wide -1 rating discount (not extended to Fair Folk, since raksha are not Exalted) and a direct cross-reference to Exalted: The Lunars p. 205 for Wyld-addiction rules. A raksha being 'addicted to the Wyld' makes little sense for a being who is Wyld-stuff herself; instead, this row cross-references this family's own Cup Grace Addiction Charms (already inventoried), which model raksha-appropriate compulsive craving and were judged the closer thematic fit.

name: Callous
summary: Selfish pragmatism over scruples and integrity; gains two bonus points per point of Virtue forfeited during character creation, cannot start with a Willpower rating more than one point higher than the sum of the two highest Virtues, and cannot have the Paragon Nature. Reinterpreted for raksha as interacting with Bedlam's per-Virtue Curses rather than the Exalted Virtue Flaw system, since that is the closest raksha equivalent.
mechanics: A character with this Flaw believes in selfish pragmatism over scruples and integrity, gaining two bonus points for every dot of Virtues forfeited during character creation. Callous characters cannot forfeit their last dot of a Virtue and may not begin play with a Willpower rating more than one point higher than the sum of their two highest Virtues, until reaching 9 total Virtue dots, at which point the Flaw is lost at no cost. Characters with this Flaw may not have the Paragon Nature (see pg-merit-true-paragon).
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; a raksha with this Flaw already faces the ordinary Bedlam Curse tied to whichever Virtue's channels run out (see virtue-bedlam-curses), the closest raksha equivalent to the Exalted Virtue Flaw the original text cross-references.
notes: REINTERPRETATION: Lunar's row notes that Exalted with this Flaw suffer the standard Exalted Virtue Flaw tied to their highest Virtue. Fair Folk have no separate Virtue Flaw system; a raksha's Virtues already trigger Bedlam and its matching Curse (see virtue-bedlam-curses) whenever a Virtue's channels are exhausted, so this Flaw's practical effect on a raksha is simply that she is more likely to burn through her Virtue channels quickly given her forfeited dots -- no additional mechanic needed to be invented.

name: Nightmares
summary: Horrific dreams whenever the character sleeps, adding 1 to the difficulty of regaining Willpower via Conviction after sleep, and inflicting lingering one-die penalties and unsoakable bashing damage on a botched Conviction roll. A purely mental Flaw with no eligibility restriction to adapt.
mechanics: A character with this Flaw experiences horrific dreams whenever she sleeps, adding 1 to the difficulty to regain Willpower with Conviction after sleep. If the roll botches, the character loses one point of temporary Willpower and suffers a one-die penalty to all non-reflexive actions for the rest of the day.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; unmodified from the Players Guide text.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-nightmares. Lunar's own notes found only a ghost-specific mechanical variant (not relevant to Fair Folk); the base Flaw carries no eligibility restriction and applies to Fair Folk exactly as written.

name: Pacifist
summary: Cannot bring himself to fight, adding 1 to the difficulty of attacks (3-pt.), or cannot attack anyone at all without spending a Willpower point to overcome his aversion for a scene (5-pt.). A purely mental Flaw with no eligibility restriction to adapt.
mechanics: For three points, a pacifist adds 1 to the difficulty of her attacks, even in self-defense. Characters with the five-point version may not attack anyone without spending a Willpower point to overcome her aversion to violence for a scene, and add 1 to the difficulty of their attacks even then.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; unmodified from the Players Guide text.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-pacifist. No splat-specific language exists anywhere in this entry; it applies to Fair Folk exactly as written.

name: Unskilled
summary: Less education and training than most adults; grants one bonus point per Ability dot forfeited during character creation, though known Favored Abilities must still meet minimum statistical requirements. Reinterpreted for raksha's own Caste Ability terminology.
mechanics: Characters with this Flaw have less education and training to draw upon than most adults, receiving one bonus point for every dot of Abilities forfeited during character creation. Characters with this Flaw must still meet the statistic requirements of all known Caste Abilities (one dot minimum, mirroring the Exalted Favored-Ability floor) and obviously cannot purchase Ability dots with bonus points.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; must still keep at least one dot in any known Caste Ability, the direct raksha equivalent of a Favored Ability floor.
notes: REINTERPRETATION: Lunar's row requires Exalted to keep at least one dot in any known Favored Ability despite this Flaw. Raksha use Caste Abilities (and, for nobles, Favored Abilities) rather than Exalted Favored Abilities alone; the one-dot floor was applied to a raksha's Caste Abilities here as the closest structural equivalent.

name: Weak-Willed
summary: Gnawing self-doubt and lack of drive; grants one bonus point per dot of permanent Willpower forfeited during character creation. Raksha take the base (non-Exalted) version, with no Willpower-4 floor, since that floor and its story-justification requirement are stated for Exalted specifically.
mechanics: A character with this Flaw suffers gnawing self-doubt and lack of drive, gaining one bonus point for every dot of permanent Willpower her player forfeits during character creation.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; may have a Willpower score as low as 2, since the Willpower-4 floor (and 2-if-also-Callous exception) is written specifically for Exalted, whom the Celestines do not Exalt as spiritual weaklings -- a framing that does not describe raksha, who are not Exalted at all.
notes: REINTERPRETATION: Lunar's row applies an Exalted-specific Willpower-4 floor (or 2 if also Callous) and a note that this Flaw is extremely rare among the Chosen. That floor's justification ('the Celestines do not Exalt spiritual weaklings') does not describe Fair Folk, who never Exalt in the first place; this row therefore uses the plain, unrestricted version of the Flaw, letting a raksha's Willpower fall as low as 2 like any non-Exalted character.

name: Barbarian
summary: Grew up outside the bounds of civilization and does not know the ways of soft city-dwellers; loses one die from all Social dice pools related to understanding or expressing civilized etiquette, and is not assumed literate unless Lore 2+. A purely social Flaw with no eligibility restriction to adapt.
mechanics: Characters with this Flaw grew up outside civilization and do not know the ways of city-dwellers, losing one die from all Social dice pools related to civilized etiquette and lacking assumed literacy unless Lore 2+.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; especially fitting for a common raksha or a chaotic Fair Folk newly settled in Creation, unfamiliar with mortal custom rather than specifically 'barbarian' custom.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-barbarian. No splat-specific language exists anywhere in this entry; it applies to Fair Folk exactly as written, and fits a raksha unfamiliar with Creation's civilized customs generally, not only literal 'barbarian' upbringing.

name: Secrets
summary: The character harbors a secret that could prove embarrassing or dangerous if others learn of it, scaling from mild embarrassment (1 pt.) up to deadly, death-penalty-worthy crimes/heresies (3 pts.). A purely social Flaw with no eligibility restriction to adapt.
mechanics: The character harbors a secret that could prove embarrassing or dangerous if discovered. For one point, it is merely inconvenient or humiliating; for two points, serious enough to invite reprisal; for three points, deadly serious, inviting death or a comparably unpleasant fate if the authorities find out.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; a raksha secretly walking Creation in a stable Mote, or a courtier plotting against her own Freehold, are natural Fair Folk-appropriate examples at the two- and three-point tiers respectively.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-secrets, whose own two-point flavor example ('Anathema living in the Imperial City') is Exalted-specific setting color. That example was replaced with raksha-appropriate equivalents (a hidden Mote-shape identity; court intrigue against one's own Freehold), since the underlying Flaw carries no eligibility restriction.

name: Disciple
summary: The character's superiors have entrusted her with a student she must train and look after, unable to abandon the relationship without permission from a higher-ranking authority; scales 1-5 points by the disciple's demands on the character's time and the consequences of the disciple's misbehavior. A purely social Flaw with no eligibility restriction to adapt.
mechanics: The character's superiors have entrusted her with a student she must train and look after, unable to abandon the relationship without permission from higher authority. The value depends on the disciple's cooperativeness and the time/consequences involved: one point for a cooperative, low-attention student; five points for an insipid, willfully malicious terror. Failure in teaching duties brings unpleasant consequences from the character's own superiors.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; fits a noble's court apprentice or a common raksha's own protege at Storyteller discretion.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-disciple, whose own flavor names Sidereals and Immaculates as most commonly having this Flaw. That framing is not relevant to Fair Folk, but the underlying Flaw carries no eligibility restriction, so it applies to Fair Folk exactly as written.

name: Enemy/Rival
summary: The character has earned the enmity of an individual or group; functions as a reverse Allies Background, with a point value matching the power of the character's foes. A purely social Flaw with no eligibility restriction to adapt.
mechanics: The character has earned the enmity of an individual or group, functioning as a reverse of the Allies Background with a matching point value. At five points, the character might contend with the wrath of a powerful god, a rival raksha court, or a similarly potent being. A rival differs from an enemy only in belonging to the character's own organization, where open action against each other invites professional reprisal.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; the five-point tier's flavor is best drawn from raksha-appropriate menaces -- a rival Freehold's ruling caste, a deep-Wyld horror, or an organized Wyld Hunt cadre -- rather than the source's Creation-specific Deathlord example.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-enemy-rival, whose five-point flavor examples (a Deathlord, a First Age survivor) are Exalted-setting color, not eligibility restrictions. This row substitutes raksha-appropriate top-tier examples while leaving the mechanic unmodified.

name: Wanted
summary: The character is a known criminal or has otherwise incurred the wrath of authorities willing to send hunters after her, regardless of actual guilt. A purely social Flaw with no eligibility restriction to adapt.
mechanics: The character is a known criminal, or her actions have incurred the wrath of authorities willing to send hunters after her, regardless of actual guilt. One point covers a minor crime (escaped slave, defaulted loan); three points, a violent crime with certain pursuit; five points, an act of inherent treason.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; the five-point tier's flavor is best drawn from raksha-appropriate treasons -- betraying one's Freehold, consorting with the Church of Balor's enemies, or the like -- rather than the source's Creation-specific Deathlord example.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-wanted, whose five-point flavor example ('consorting with the Deathlords') is Exalted-setting color, not an eligibility restriction. This row substitutes a raksha-appropriate top-tier example while leaving the mechanic unmodified.

name: Disturbing
summary: The character makes others uncomfortable through an indefinable aura of menace (not necessarily ugliness or rudeness), adding 1 or 2 to the difficulty of all Social rolls not based on intimidation. A purely social Flaw that fits a raksha's inherently uncanny nature especially well.
mechanics: Characters with this Flaw make others uncomfortable, exuding an indefinable aura of menace. For two points, this adds 1 to the difficulty of all Social rolls not based on intimidation; for three points, the penalty increases to 2. Most people give the character a wide berth and minimize contact even when no Social roll is at stake.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; unmodified from the Players Guide text.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-disturbing. No splat-specific language exists anywhere in this entry; it applies to Fair Folk exactly as written, and suits a raksha's fundamentally alien nature especially well even while wearing a stable Mote.

name: Child
summary: The character has not yet reached full maturity; most adults treat him with patronizing amusement or disdain and generally ignore his opinions. A purely social Flaw that fits a raksha wearing a child-shaped Mote.
mechanics: The character has not yet reached full maturity, and most adults treat him with patronizing amusement or disdain, generally ignoring his opinions. The character loses one to three dice from all Social rolls involving interactions with adults, depending on the adult's tolerance. Most children also have the Small Flaw and a measure of Unskilled.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble, wearing a child-shaped Mote or genuinely newly coalesced from the Wyld; pairs naturally with pg-flaw-small and pg-flaw-unskilled as the source text notes.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-child. No splat-specific language exists anywhere in this entry; it applies to Fair Folk exactly as written, whether representing a raksha whose chosen Mote is a child's body or one genuinely newly formed and inexperienced.

name: Damaged Artifact
summary: An Artifact owned through the Artifact Background has suffered damage that impairs its function, scaling from minor damage (1 pt.) up to near-total damage (3 pts., presently useless but repairable). Points gained cannot exceed the Background/bonus points spent obtaining the artifact, minus at least one remaining point of Artifact rating. Applies directly to raksha, whose own Artifact Background purchases glamour spells, behemoths, adjurations and Wyld artifacts rather than Five-Magical-Materials items.
mechanics: One of the mystical wonders owned by the character through the Artifact Background has suffered damage, either in the past or since falling into her possession. One point indicates minor damage (a weapon loses a point of damage or accuracy, armor loses soak, or a complicated device functions with reduced reliability); two points, major damage (five points from weapons/armor, or half effectiveness for complicated devices); three points, near-total damage (the artifact is presently useless, though repairable through a proportionally complex and expensive process). Players may not gain more points from this Flaw than the Background/bonus points spent obtaining the artifact, whichever is less, and must retain at least one more point of Artifact than the points obtained here.
compatibility: Any raksha with the Artifact Background, common or noble; per artifact-background-fair-folk's own dot table, the maximum Flaw-point cap is set by however many Artifact Background dots the raksha actually spent on the specific glamour spell, behemoth, adjuration or Wyld artifact being damaged, exactly as the original worked example compares Solar and Abyssal Artifact costs against each other.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-damaged-artifact, whose worked example compares Solar and Abyssal Artifact Background point costs for the same item. Raksha use their own, structurally different Artifact Background (artifact-background-fair-folk, purchasing glamour spells, behemoths, adjurations and Wyld artifacts rather than Five-Magical-Materials items), so the same cross-splat cost-comparison principle -- the Flaw's cap is set by whatever the raksha herself spent to obtain the specific item -- was preserved without importing the Solar/Abyssal worked example verbatim.

name: Debt
summary: The character owes money or goods to an individual or organization of substantial power, functioning as an inverse Resources Background with an identical rating system. Reinterpreted for raksha as an inverse Gossamer Background, since Fair Folk do not use the Resources Background at all.
requirements: None beyond the ordinary Gossamer Background rating scale (0-5) this Flaw inverts.
mechanics: The character owes wealth to an individual or organization of substantial power -- for a raksha, most plausibly another raksha court, a Freehold's ruling caste, or a powerful gossamer-broker. She must either pay regular installments with interest or promise a full repayment by an agreed date; failure brings hunters or worse. This Flaw functions as an inverse of the character's wealth Background with an identical rating system, so a character with four points of Debt owes a sum equal to Gossamer 4. Characters may hold both Debt and their wealth Background simultaneously, provided Debt exceeds it; buying off Debt with wealth accumulated in play costs no experience.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; reinterpreted from the original inverse-Resources mechanic to an inverse-Gossamer mechanic (see gossamer-background), since raksha exclude the Resources Background entirely (see followers-and-resources-excluded-fair-folk) in favor of Gossamer.
notes: JUDGMENT CALL / REINTERPRETATION: this Flaw is explicitly defined as an inverse of the Resources Background, which raksha do not have (see followers-and-resources-excluded-fair-folk). Rather than excluding the Flaw outright, it was reinterpreted against Gossamer -- raksha's own wealth-and-influence Background (gossamer-background) -- using the identical 1-5 rating mechanic the original text describes, since Gossamer plays the same structural role for raksha that Resources plays for Creation-born characters.

name: Unbidden Oracle
summary: At least once per story but no more than once per scene, the character unintentionally speaks prophetic words of ill omen, invariably at the most inopportune moment; such prophecies almost always come true. Included for Fair Folk with a flagged conceptual tension, since the mechanism is framed as a Bureau of Destiny phenomenon correcting Creation-bound Essence disruption -- a Loom-of-Fate process raksha stand outside of.
mechanics: At least once per story, but no more than once per scene, a character with this Flaw speaks prophetic words of ill omen without meaning to, invariably at the most inopportune moment. Such prophecies almost always come true, or would if the warning hadn't prompted countermeasures. A point of Willpower can prevent an outburst, but prophecies of real importance eventually find their way out regardless.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; included as selectable since no eligibility restriction is stated, though the mechanism's own Bureau of Destiny framing sits oddly for a being of the Wyld -- see pg-merit-destiny's notes for the fuller Fate/Loom conceptual discussion applying here too.
notes: JUDGMENT CALL: like pg-merit-destiny above, this Flaw's underlying mechanism (the Bureau of Destiny correcting dooms from ambient Essence disruption within Creation's Loom of Fate) is a Creation-bound cosmic process that sits oddly for a raksha, who is native to the Wyld outside that Loom. The Players Guide text names no eligibility restriction, so this row is included as selectable rather than excluded by inference, but the tension is flagged here for Storyteller awareness -- a raksha oracle would most plausibly be one who has spent significant time settled within Creation.

name: Dark Fate
summary: No matter how heroic her deeds, the character will ultimately suffer or bring about some great tragedy at its appointed time, defying even the Maidens' intervention; severity scales from a lifetime of petty miseries or a painful demise (1 pt.) to epic, empire-crumbling catastrophe (5 pts.). No splat is excluded except Sidereals (normally exempt via their Bureau of Destiny role), so Fair Folk are fully eligible, though the same Loom-of-Fate conceptual tension flagged for Destiny applies here too.
mechanics: No happy ending awaits a character with Dark Fate. No matter how heroic her deeds, she shall ultimately suffer or bring about some great tragedy at its appointed time, defying the most potent sorcery, astrology and divine intervention short of the Maidens themselves. Severity scales from a one-point doom (a violent demise or a lifetime of petty miseries) to a five-point doom (epic, empire-crumbling catastrophe). Those fated for ruin seldom know the curse they bear, though ill portents typically accompany their birth; astrologers can sense the presence of doom with a single success, though identifying its specifics is much harder. Cursed characters receive the same coincidental protection as those with positive Destiny (see pg-merit-destiny) until their doom's appointed time.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble, at the full 1-5 pt. range; the only named exclusion (Sidereals, normally exempt via their Bureau of Destiny role) does not apply to Fair Folk, though a raksha's Dark Fate sits within the same Loom-of-Fate conceptual tension flagged in pg-merit-destiny's notes. The Celestial-Exalted-specific 'passes to the next incarnation' clause does not apply, since raksha have no reincarnating-Essence mechanic.
notes: JUDGMENT CALL: only Sidereals are explicitly excluded from this Flaw (they are normally exempt via their Bureau of Destiny role); no restriction is stated against Fair Folk. This row drops the Celestial-Exalted-specific clause about passing the doom to a next incarnation, since raksha have no such mechanic, but otherwise applies the Flaw unmodified. See pg-merit-destiny's notes for the same Fate/Loom conceptual tension that applies here.

name: Unlucky
summary: The character suffers an endless stream of purposeless misfortune (unlike Dark Fate, this has no ultimate destiny behind it). The Storyteller gets a negative luck pool spendable to force rerolls of the character's rolls or to negatively bias games of chance. A purely mechanical Flaw with no eligibility restriction to adapt.
mechanics: A character with this Flaw suffers an endless stream of purposeless misfortune. The Storyteller receives a negative luck pool equal to the points invested, spendable to force a reroll of the character's own roll (keeping the worse result) or to negatively bias a game of chance. Characters may be simultaneously Lucky (see pg-merit-lucky) and Unlucky, since the Storyteller and player spend their respective pools independently. The negative pool refreshes at the end of every story.
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; unmodified from the Players Guide text.
notes: Derived from Lunar's pg-flaw-unlucky. No splat-specific language exists anywhere in this entry; it applies to Fair Folk exactly as written, and can stack with pg-merit-lucky exactly as documented.

name: Weak Essence
summary: The character suffers stunted magical development (or is newly coalesced), reducing starting Essence rating to 1 and severely limiting Charm selection. A near-perfect fit for Fair Folk: the book explicitly extends this Flaw to any 'other magical being whose baseline starting Essence is 2,' and every raksha -- common or noble -- starts with Essence 2.
mechanics: Individuals with this Flaw suffer stunted magical development, or perhaps recently came into being. This reduces the character's starting Essence rating to 1, severely limiting Grace Charm selection (since a raksha's single Essence pool equals permanent Essence x 10, an Essence-1 raksha has only 10 motes to work with). The player may withhold up to five Charms in reserve, typically until Essence can be raised in play; withheld Charms waive their experience cost but still require the same training time (though Fair Folk have no training-time delay at all -- see fair-folk-experience-and-training-time).
compatibility: Any raksha, common or noble; the book's own text extends this Flaw to 'other magical beings' with a normal starting Essence of 2, which describes every raksha exactly, per fair-folk-creation-overview-noble / -common.
notes: STRONG FIT: unlike most of this chapter's Exalted-specific language, this Flaw's own text explicitly and by design extends beyond Exalted to 'other magical beings,' provided their normal starting Essence is 2 (excepting Dragon Kings). Fair Folk's own creation rules (fair-folk-creation-overview-noble / -common) state 'Essence starts at 2' for every raksha, common or noble alike, making this one of the cleanest, least-reinterpreted fits in the entire derived set. The 'newly-Exalted' framing was softened to 'newly coalesced' to fit a being who never Exalts, and the training-time clause was cross-referenced against this family's own rule that raksha have no training-time delay at all.

name: Ghost Cestus (Artifact •••)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: an armored fighting glove (cestus) enchanted with orichalcum, moonsilver, starstone, or (most commonly) jade so its punches and grapples can strike and subdue spirits, ghosts, and gods who are normally untouchable to mortal fists.
requirements: None (usable by mortals, magicians, sorcerers, or any Exalt without special training).
mechanics: Ghost cesti work against umbrood and ghosts just as well as against normal humans, requiring no special training to use. When a character fights using ghost cesti, the player makes all the normal dice rolls for unarmed combat and inflicts the normal, Strength-based damage of the combat maneuver, but instead of health levels, the character inflicts points of temporary Willpower loss on the spirit target (see Exalted core rulebook p. 147 for the total effects of Willpower loss on spirits/humans). The victim can soak this attack using her own Willpower. Spirits reduced to 0 Willpower this way become totally obedient to whoever subdued them. Spirits and mortals both recover lost Willpower from this effect as if it were bashing damage. Ghost cesti cannot outright kill a spirit -- that requires more dreadful and powerful magic -- but a cestus-wielding warrior or wizard can pummel even a powerful spirit into submission, since spirits are unused to taking uppercuts from 'mere mortals.'
compatibility: Any wielder, worn on a physical hand -- mortal, magician, sorcerer, or Exalt of any splat, or a raksha wearing a Mote shaped with the requisite fingers and knuckles; a local spirit challenged the Empress's authority once and she sent a champion armed with ghost cesti to subdue it, and non-Exalted priests of the Immaculate Order also carry ghost cesti.
notes: Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'Ghost Cestus (Artifact •••)', printed pp. 77-78 (PDF 78-79). Universal/cross-splat catalog entry; derived from Lunar's already-verified transcription of this same universal chapter (docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json, id artifact-ghost-cestus) -- identical id, name, mechanics, cost, and citation, per this pass's brief. This is purely a worn physical item requiring no Essence, Charm, or Exaltation to operate, so it transfers to Fair Folk without reinterpretation: a raksha would purchase it through the Artifact Background (see artifact-background-fair-folk) exactly as she would any other three-dot artifact, and could wear/wield it on whichever Mote she currently inhabits like any other physical glove. No genuine incompatibility found; raksha are explicitly capable of owning Five-Magical-Materials artifacts per artifact-background-fair-folk's own dot table, just rarely in practice.

name: Sling Bow of Ice (Artifact •••)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: a bow-and-sling hybrid weapon common in the First Age, made of mingled black and blue jade, that fires bullets or bolts which explode on impact into a cloud of snow and shivering, uncontrollable cold, freezing the ground and everyone nearby.
requirements: An Essence-manipulating wielder (the weapon itself is inert in the hands of a mortal with no Essence to fuel it).
mechanics: A sling bow resembles a normal bow, but instead of arrows it fires bullets of stone or metal, or a sling. These particular sling bows are fashioned of mingled black and blue jade carved with a fine tracery of frost ferns. A bolt of black or blue jade fired from the weapon explodes on impact into a cloud of snow and ice that sets everyone within 20 feet shivering uncontrollably, no matter how warmly they are dressed, unless they carry a bit of orichalcum or are protected by magic that shields them from cold. It also coats the ground with a thin layer of slippery ice, making it hard to remain upright. The Sling Bow requires a single mote of Essence to fuel its magic; the wielder rolls Essence + Archery. For each success, everyone within 10 feet of the impact loses one dot of Dexterity from frostbitten numbness and slipping on the icy ground; a character reduced to 0 Dexterity can do nothing but huddle in misery. A character's Essence is subtracted from the number of successes rolled. The supernatural cold lasts one turn per success rolled in mild weather, and five minutes per success if the weather is already chill. Anyone who enters the zone regains Dexterity per turn; anyone who leaves it regains Dexterity per turn. A character may soak the cold using her Essence rating; the weapon does not affect Undead at all. A person who carries a bit of orichalcum, or characters with charms or spells that protect them from extreme cold, become immune to the effect. In the First Age, soldiers operating alongside Sling Bow-armed Exalted wore orichalcum rings to protect themselves from the weapon's effect; since the art of forging orichalcum was lost centuries ago, latter-day warriors must exercise care when employing the Bow.
compatibility: Any Essence-manipulating wielder, raksha included -- every raksha has an Essence rating (starting at 2) and a mote pool (Essence x 10) exactly like the Creation-born Exalted (see fair-folk-creation-overview-common / -noble), so a raksha wearing a Mote with hands to draw a bow qualifies without reinterpretation; historically used by General Tepet Hala in the Great Eastern War, where it drove the Eastern Army across a river and let him take the enemy army by surprise.
notes: Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'Sling Bow of Ice (Artifact •••)', printed p. 78 (PDF 79). Universal/cross-splat catalog entry; derived from Lunar's already-verified transcription of this same universal chapter (docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json, id artifact-sling-bow-of-ice) -- identical id, name, mechanics, cost, and citation, per this pass's brief. No genuine incompatibility found: the weapon's 'Essence-manipulating wielder' requirement is satisfied by any raksha's own Essence rating and mote pool, and 'a single mote of Essence' spent to fire it is the same lowercase-mote currency raksha already spend on Grace Charms -- not to be confused with a raksha's Mote (capitalized), the physical body/shell she wears in Creation, which is simply what holds and draws the bow.

name: The Golden Viper (Artifact •••••)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: a First Age automaton shaped like a six-foot orichalcum-and-jewel serpent, intelligent enough to speak and advise its owner, that serves whoever possesses it and can transmute a bite victim's flesh into gold.
requirements: Ownership of the Viper following the death of its previous owner (it serves anyone who possesses it once its prior master has died).
mechanics: The Golden Viper is the most intelligent automaton known, and even First Age texts speak of it as a notable relic. This lifelike serpent, fashioned of orichalcum and jewels in a framework of starstone, stretches six feet long and is about four inches thick at its thickest. The Viper serves anyone who possesses it once its previous owner is dead. The Viper is a formidable assassin: it can move through small openings and strikes like a real serpent, coiling and lashing out. In a matter of seconds, a person bitten by the Viper turns to gold (ordinary gold, not orichalcum). Magicians and Exalted have somewhat greater resistance to the Viper's bite than do more mortal folk, but even they can be slain and transmuted. The automaton knows whatever any of its clients knew; it advises its owner on the basis of this truly awesome base of stolen knowledge and experience. The Golden Viper knows no mercy or compassion; it advises the most ruthlessly practical course whatever goal its master seeks. If the Viper's master is not already a complete cynic by human nature, she will after a few years of the Viper's callous insight into human foibles. System: Attributes: Strength 3, Stamina 5, Perception 5, Intelligence 7, Wits 5, Charisma 3, Manipulation 5, Appearance 3, Willpower 10. It lacks Virtues since these have no meaning for its cold, inhuman intellect. Instead of a list of specific Abilities, the Storyteller may assume that it has a rating of 4 in any Ability it needs, with one exception: it remembers nothing about the First Age -- or claims not to. It speaks all known languages, and rapidly learns any new one it is exposed to. Its bite inflicts a base of 6L special damage; only armor can soak this damage, though Exalted can add their Essence to their soak rating. Each health level inflicted also strips away one point of Dexterity, as the victim stiffens, and it has a soak of 7L/10B. Its health levels are -0x3/-1x2/-2x2/-4x2/Incap x3. Restoring a health level lost to the Golden Viper is a difficulty 2 task on an Intelligence + Crafts roll.
compatibility: Any owner who acquires it after its previous owner's death, raksha included -- a raksha wearing a Mote is a genuine possessor in exactly the same sense as any mortal or Exalted owner; functions as an autonomous intelligent servant/assassin rather than a wielded or attuned item, and the text's own carve-out that 'Exalted can add their Essence to their soak rating' extends equally to a raksha's Essence rating.
notes: Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'The Golden Viper (Artifact •••••)', printed p. 78 (PDF 79). Universal/cross-splat catalog entry; derived from Lunar's already-verified transcription of this same universal chapter (docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json, id artifact-the-golden-viper) -- identical id, name, mechanics, cost, and citation, per this pass's brief. Statted as an intelligent construct/NPC-style artifact (Attributes, health levels, bite damage) rather than a worn/wielded item with a mote cost. No genuine incompatibility found: 'any owner...once its previous owner is dead' places no restriction on species or Exaltation status, and a raksha's Essence rating (see fair-folk-creation-overview-common / -noble) fills the same 'Exalted can add their Essence to their soak rating' clause the source text carves out for Exalted victims.

name: Land Ship (Artifact •••••)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: an extremely rare First Age vessel with a keel of interleaved yellow and black jade that lets it sail across dry land as if it were water, powered by an Essence-manipulating captain and crew.
requirements: An Essence-manipulating captain to sail it (First Age devices existed that stored Essence so a land ship could sail without an Exalted crew, but these devices have all been lost or destroyed).
mechanics: In the First Age, land ships were common. Very few of them remain -- masters of earth and water magic, working together, could craft new land ships, but this has not happened in centuries. Although land ships were once rare, war or accident has destroyed most of them; two Dragon-Blooded nobles own land ships, so does one Deathlord, and perhaps a few more await discovery. All the magic of a land ship rests in its keel -- a long, curving strip of yellow jade sandwiched between strips of black jade. The rest of the ship is ordinary wood and metal, built however the shipwright pleased, and subject to normal wear and aging. The two land ships in mortal hands are both single-masted forty-footers with high prows, one square-rigged and the other lateen-rigged; the Deathlord's ship is a 60-foot sloop. System: A land ship requires someone who can manipulate Essence to start it sailing on land, though in the First Age there were devices that contained Essence that could be used so that the vessels did not need Exalted crews. To start the vessel sailing requires one mote of Essence per hour and a simple success on an Essence + Sailing roll. With a good wind and a skilled crew, a land ship can sail 10 miles per hour, +1 mph for each success on the captain's Intelligence + Sailing roll -- wind permitting. Bad weather or obstacles such as trees or boulders result in increased difficulty. A land ship's magic has its limits: a land ship cannot sail up or down cliffs, any more than a mundane ship can sail up or down a waterfall. The one time someone tried using a land ship to breach castle walls, the ship's high prow went into the wall -- and the liquefied stone pushed the ship down into the earth. The land ship sank into the earth.
cost: 1 mote per hour of sailing (plus an Essence + Sailing roll to begin)
compatibility: Any Essence-manipulating captain, raksha included -- a raksha's Essence rating and mote pool (see fair-folk-creation-overview-common / -noble) satisfy the requirement exactly as any Exalt, sorcerer, or other Essence-wielding pilot would; currently known to be owned by two Dragon-Blooded noble houses and one Deathlord.
notes: Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'Land Ship (Artifact •••••)', printed p. 79 (PDF 80). Universal/cross-splat catalog entry; derived from Lunar's already-verified transcription of this same universal chapter (docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json, id artifact-land-ship) -- identical id, name, mechanics, cost, and citation, per this pass's brief. No genuine incompatibility found; a raksha wearing a seaworthy (or land-worthy) Mote could crew and captain this ship exactly as any other Essence-manipulating pilot, and would purchase it through the Artifact Background like any other five-dot artifact (see artifact-background-fair-folk), rare as that is for a raksha in practice.

name: Singing Staff (Artifact ••••)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: a man-high staff of white jade, played with a rosined bow like a musical saw, that reshapes earth, sand, clay, or stone into whatever form its music evokes -- as useful for digging canals as for toppling castle walls.
requirements: An Essence-manipulating player skilled in Performance (even in the First Age, a Singing Staff required an Exalted wielder).
mechanics: The Singing Staff demonstrates the odd approach to magic taken by some First Age magicians. This man-high staff of white jade is carved in an irregular series of waves and swellings, with a knob at each end. When rubbed with a rosined bow, the Singing Staff emits a tone, like a musical saw; different parts of the staff play different pitches and timbres. If one plants the end of the Staff on the ground and plays it correctly, the land responds to the music, rising and falling like waves or shaping itself like clay molded by unseen hands. This makes the Singing Staff precious as both a tool and a weapon: the Staff's uses are limited only by the skill of its player. Singing Staves are immensely sophisticated devices, despite their simple appearance. They were never easy to make, and in the modern era are vastly more difficult -- only three are known to exist: one is in the hands of the Empress and stored among her personal effects, one is held by the Immaculates of Paisep for study, and one was lost in battle with the Tepet legions and now lies on the bottom of the Inner Sea. Although the effects of the Staves are functionally identical, each has its own musical 'tuning.' System: Wielding the Staff's magic costs one mote of Essence per turn, and even in the First Age required an Exalted wielder. Each turn of use, the Staff can reshape 100 cubic feet of earth, sand, or clay, or 20 cubic feet of stone.
