To use the Staff, the character's player must succeed on an Essence + Performance roll (difficulty set by the detail or magnitude of the task). The Storyteller may demand multiple rolls to succeed at lengthy tasks, or additional Ability rolls for tasks that demand specialized training. For instance, constructing an ornamental stone pavilion might require three Essence + Ability rolls to use the Staff correctly, plus another Craft roll to get the ornamental carving right.
compatibility: Any Essence-manipulating wielder with Performance skill, raksha included -- a raksha's Essence rating and mote pool (see fair-folk-creation-overview-common / -noble) satisfy the 'even in the First Age required an Exalted wielder' requirement in the same way as any Exalt or Essence-wielding magician, so long as she has Performance to bring to the Essence + Performance roll; the three known Staves are held by the Empress, the Immaculate Order (for study), and one was lost when the Tepet legions were defeated and now rests at the bottom of the Inner Sea.
notes: Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'Singing Staff (Artifact ••••)', printed pp. 79-80 (PDF 80-81). Universal/cross-splat catalog entry; derived from Lunar's already-verified transcription of this same universal chapter (docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json, id artifact-singing-staff) -- identical id, name, mechanics, cost, and citation, per this pass's brief. 'Paisep' transcribed as printed, matching Lunar's flagged best-effort reading of a hard-to-make-out scanned place name (see Lunar's own notes field for this row). No genuine incompatibility found; the source text's 'required an Exalted wielder' language is satisfied by a raksha's own Essence rating exactly as it is for Sidereal's derived copy of this same row.

name: Eye of Autochthon (Artifact N/A)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: an immense black pearl created by the Primordial Autochthon that suppresses all physical and magical turbulence for miles around and grants its wielder god-like, Storyteller-adjudicated reality-editing power over Manses, Demesnes, and the stable lands of Creation.
requirements: None stated beyond possession; using it to perform any specific effect requires an Essence + Occult roll (see mechanics).
mechanics: The Eye of Autochthon surpasses all other magic items known, having been itself created by the Primordial Autochthon. Through the Eye, mortals can tap a tiny fraction of a power older than the world or gods or time itself -- if they dare. The Eye looks like an immense black pearl, so large that a hero might strain to wrap his arms around it. Its ebon luster draws the eye into limitless depths of dark surface, a void that could birth worlds. No force, whether natural or divine, could so much as scratch the Eye's surface, but in the First Age some unknown agency clamped the great globe into a tight-fitting nest of gimbaled rings so that the Eye could turn freely in all directions, with no need to hand-push it; nevertheless it spins by itself. System: The Eye's active powers can be summarized as a 'plot device': it can do whatever the Storyteller wants it to; in general, its history shows it can create, destroy, or usurp control of Manses and Demesnes, and can transform the stable lands of the Realm and Threshold, though it cannot transform the looser, more Essence-soaked reality of the Wyld or the shadowlands. Its passive power to suppress all disturbances of land, sea, air, and magical turbulence for a league around it operates automatically and needs no roll: no wind blows above a mild, steady breeze, no one in the area suffers Wyld contamination, charms and sorcery have normal immediate effects but any continuing effect has its duration cut in half as the Eye reorders local Essence, and magical storms, waves, and earthquakes fail or stabilize. The Eye demands great expenditure of Essence: usurping control of a Manse, for instance, might require the player to expend 15 motes for every dot of the Manse's power (how an un-Exalted prophet once used it remains a mystery). The Eye also demands great skill to use: the player must succeed at an Essence + Occult roll at +2 difficulty to discover a new use for the Eye, and roll a simple success to perform that same feat thereafter. Any botch means the character suffers some bizarre and very permanent doom -- possibly affecting everyone within a mile or so, depending on the Storyteller's mood. The Eye does not function as an instant enemy-killer: the Primordial's power does not operate on so focused a scale, and any target smaller than a castle is too puny for the Eye to affect directly.
cost: Variable (e.g. 15 motes per dot of a Manse's power to usurp it); Essence + Occult roll at +2 difficulty to learn a new use, simple success thereafter
compatibility: Any possessor, Exalted or not (an un-Exalted prophet, Ikerre, once wielded it) -- this explicit 'not' carve-out covers a raksha wearing a Mote at least as well as it covers an ordinary mortal, and the Eye's passive suppression of magical turbulence would blunt a raksha's own Wyld-native powers exactly as it blunts anyone else's within a league of it, a genuinely notable interaction worth flagging even though it does not bar ownership; a Storyteller-adjudicated 'plot device' artifact rather than a routinely player-purchasable Background item -- best used as a rare, campaign-defining relic rather than a starting-character purchase.
notes: Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'Eye of Autochthon (Artifact N/A)', printed p. 80 (PDF 81), the last entry in the chapter and the last mechanical content in the book (PDF p. 82 is the inside/outside back cover). Universal/cross-splat catalog entry; derived from Lunar's already-verified transcription of this same universal chapter (docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json, id artifact-eye-of-autochthon) -- identical id, name, mechanics, cost, and citation, per this pass's brief. Rated 'N/A' in the source rather than a numeric Artifact dot rating, reflecting its explicit framing as a Storyteller plot device; recorded as a 'selectable' catalog row here matching Lunar's and Sidereal's own best-judgment call (since it is nonetheless a genuine named artifact a character could conceivably acquire), rather than 'gm-only'. FLAGGED INTERACTION (not a blocking incompatibility): the Eye's passive league-wide suppression of 'magical turbulence' plausibly overlaps with a raksha's own Wyld-derived nature (see innate-powers-wyld-immunity) in ways the source text never anticipated for a non-Exalted, non-mortal owner or bystander; this is noted as an open interpretive question for a future Storyteller to resolve, not resolved here, since the source book gives no guidance either way and raksha are outside its scope entirely.

name: Cargo Preservation Spindles (Artifact • to •••, Depending on Size)
summary: A set of four five-sided jade spindles, planted in the corners of a hold or cabin, that magically preserves any cargo placed within their protected area from rot, vermin, water damage, and shifting in heavy seas -- larger spindle sets protect larger spaces.
requirements: None beyond ownership; using them requires no Essence, Charm, or roll, only physically planting the four spindles and 'introducing' the cargo to be protected.
mechanics: Cargo preservation spindles come in a set of four, ranging in size from slender spires a handbreadth high to slender pillars nearly as tall as a man; despite the size difference, all are the same basic five-sided form, coming to a sharp point at either end. The shorter end of each spindle is set into a socket carved into the decking, or a specially placed holder (like a candlestick) for the smaller sizes; one spindle is placed in each corner of the room or hold to be protected. The size of the spindles determines how much area they protect: small spindles cover only a room the size of a typical passenger's cabin, while the tallest sets protect a large cargo hold. To use the spindles, the owner first 'introduces' the cargo to be protected by pressing the long end of each spindle into the corresponding corner of the room (far enough to leave a mark, not far enough to damage the crate or contents); the contents are described to the spindles in general detail, and the magic allows some variation, but radically different materials from those described will not be protected -- a smuggler who tries to hide contraband among a legitimate cargo will find the hidden freight ruined while the rest stays intact. Once introduced, the cargo is protected from nearly all forms of damage: food will not rot, spoil, or be eaten by vermin (though food removed from its container ages normally); water, even heavy brine, cannot affect the goods; crates stay in place under all but the heaviest seas and, even if toppled, their contents remain undamaged; and fire cannot take hold within the protected area. The spindles do not prevent theft outright, but anyone touching a protected crate or package immediately knows if anything has been taken from it. Protection lasts only as long as the cargo remains within the spindles' warded hold or room; goods removed from that protection are once again subject to normal spoilage. The spindles themselves are not easy to make: carefully prized shards of all five types of jade are bound together with bands of orichalcum and pins of moonsilver, each facet carved with the symbol of the Elemental Dragon whose aspect watches over and protects the warded contents.
compatibility: Any owner, with no splat restriction stated in the source; a purely passive, physical artifact requiring no Essence, Charm, or Exaltation to use, so it transfers to Fair Folk without reinterpretation -- a raksha would purchase a set through the Artifact Background exactly as any other one-to-three-dot artifact and could plant/use the spindles with ordinary Mote hands like any mortal crew member.
notes: Chapter Four: Creatures, Gods, Charms and Artifacts, 'Artifacts of the Waves' section opener, printed pp. 123-124 (PDF 124-125), transcribed directly from the rendered PDF pages (this book has no text layer). This entry precedes the task brief's own list of 'already-confirmed' artifacts on this page and was found during the required cover-to-cover read of pp. 123-128; it carries no splat restriction of any kind in the source text (unlike several of this section's later, Essence-costed artifacts), making it one of the cleanest fits for Fair Folk in this batch. Not to be confused with the mundane, non-Artifact-rated Heavy/Superheavy/Shore Fire Cannon entries on the facing column of printed p. 123 (PDF 124), which are Resources-purchased ship weapons rather than Artifacts and were deliberately left out of scope per the task's Artifact-only brief.

name: Armor of Aquatic Puissance (Artifact ••••)
summary: A suit of articulated plate armor heavily inlaid with sparkling blue jade, dating to before the Contagion, that lets its wearer breathe underwater, freely adjust buoyancy, swim at double speed with no penalty, and see clearly underwater, while keeping its full soak against attacks made beneath the waves.
requirements: None stated beyond ownership and wearing the armor (the breathing effect draws on the wearer's own Stamina + Endurance, not Essence).
mechanics: Soak: 10L/12B. Mobility Penalty: -2/0. Fatigue Value 1. Commitment: 8. These curious suits of articulated plate armor appear not so much to be forged as carved. Regardless of what type of metal the armor is made of, it is heavily inlaid with a rare form of sparkling blue jade that shifts as it wears, even in the sun; the armor is built to tolerances and stresses that cannot be duplicated today, and all known suits date from before the Contagion. The helm is a single piece of blue jade that locks under the shoulder yoke with a twist; the whole armor, excepting the faceplate, is carved in an ornate pattern of scales and fins to resemble the face of a fierce, bearded, angry warrior. Although not as strong as other enchanted articulated plate, it has advantages that make it extremely useful to anyone who spends much time on the water. Most importantly, with the helm locked in place the wearer can breathe normally even in the deepest waters; the armor does not address other needs (food, water, etc.), so this effect can only be sustained for Stamina + Endurance hours in a row before the helm must be removed. The wearer can alter the armor's buoyancy at will, surfacing or sinking without penalty; the armor doubles the wearer's normal underwater swimming rate and the wearer suffers no mobility penalties underwater, and can swim on the surface as fast as he moves on land (although ranged combat remains just as difficult as it would be without the armor). The wearer sees underwater just as if in open air (clouds of silt, squid ink, and similar materials still block vision, as fog or smoke would above water). The armor has sockets for two hearthstones. Although not as common as some other enchanted armors, a fair number of suits survive: both the Imperial navy and the forces of Lookshy are known to have several, more aquatically inclined Dynastic houses each have at least a couple, several more are rumored to be held by the Guild, and the Lintha pirates are known to have at least two. Outcastes working as pirates or merchants may own others but are quiet about it if so; no Abyssal is known to own a suit (unsurprisingly), though deathknights have comparable suits of their own design and manufacture.
compatibility: Any wearer, with no splat restriction stated beyond the passing note that no Abyssal is known to own one (a social/setting fact about who currently holds surviving suits, not a mechanical exclusion); a raksha wearing a Mote shaped to fit articulated plate could wear and benefit from this armor exactly as any mortal or Exalted owner, drawing on her own Stamina + Endurance for the breathing effect rather than Essence.
notes: Chapter Four: Creatures, Gods, Charms and Artifacts, 'Artifacts of the Waves' section, 'Armor of Aquatic Puissance (Artifact ••••)', printed p. 124 (PDF 125), transcribed directly from the rendered PDF page (this book has no text layer). This matches the task brief's 'already-confirmed' listing for this page. No genuine incompatibility found: the armor's key effects (breathing, buoyancy, swim speed, underwater vision, soak) are all passive properties of the armor itself keyed to the wearer's own physical Attributes (Stamina + Endurance), not to Essence, Charms, or Exaltation, so a raksha's Mote wears it exactly like a mortal or Exalted body would.

name: Steelsilk Sails (Artifact ••)
summary: Rare sails woven from spider silk and gossamer moonsilver, prized for speed and agility in the wind and near-total durability in battle, since steel weapons, fire, arrows, and other mundane attacks all fail to damage them.
requirements: None beyond ownership and rigging the sails to a ship; purely passive, no Essence or roll needed to benefit from their properties.
mechanics: Highly sought after by those who favor speed and agility in the wind and durability in battle, these rare sails are supposedly made out of the silk of wood spiders or other spider spirits. Gossamer fine and light but strong as metal, steelsilk is nonetheless very stiff and makes poor armor. Steelsilk sails add +1 to all Sail rolls for keeping control of the ship in a storm or for gaining or losing speed, and they allow a ship to sail two points closer to the wind and are all but impenetrable by mundane weapons: a ballista might punch a hole in a steelsilk sail, but swords, arrows, javelins, and other weapons are useless against them. Sails made of steelsilk have 15B/10L soak, take 20 health levels to damage, and 40 to destroy; they take only half damage from wind, waves, and fire. Repairing steelsilk sails requires a Charm or the Crack-Mending Technique; no other way is known today to mend steelsilk once it is damaged.
compatibility: Any owner, with no splat restriction stated in the source; a purely passive property of the sail cloth itself, unrelated to who commands or crews the ship, so it transfers to Fair Folk without reinterpretation -- a raksha-owned or raksha-crewed vessel could be rigged with steelsilk sails exactly like any other ship.
notes: Chapter Four: Creatures, Gods, Charms and Artifacts, 'Artifacts of the Waves' section, 'Steelsilk Sails (Artifact ••)', printed p. 124 (PDF 125), transcribed directly from the rendered PDF page (this book has no text layer). Matches the task brief's 'already-confirmed' listing for this page. No genuine incompatibility found: this is a ship-fitting property, not a worn or wielded item requiring a particular kind of bearer, so it applies identically regardless of who owns or crews the vessel.

name: Storm Sapphire (Artifact ••• for Lesser Stones or •••• for the Black Stones)
summary: A giant sapphire (green and light blue being the weakest, black the most powerful) that can quell a storm at sea, at the cost of the user's own motes, Willpower, and health levels -- the darkest stones can dispel any storm, but the wielder never knows in advance how much of herself the storm will demand.
requirements: An Essence-manipulating wielder (Exalted, spirit, or god-blooded) able to power the stone with motes, Willpower, and unsoakable health levels.
mechanics: Storm sapphires are giant sapphires, most the size of a man's fist or larger. The most powerful are black, but they come in all colors, with green (the least powerful) being the most common. Storm sapphires have the power to quell storms, calming the sea and sky even under the most savage conditions, but this power does not come without a cost: to stop a storm, the wielder must power the sapphire with her own life force, paying motes of Essence, Willpower, and health levels as shown on the Storm Sapphire Effect Table below (cost rises with storm strength, from a plain 'Storm' up to the catastrophic 'Island Killer'). These health levels cannot be soaked or reduced for the stone to work properly, though they heal normally afterward. Storm Sapphire Effect Table (cost to quell storm; Blue/Green Sapphire vs. Black Sapphire): Storm -- 20 motes/2 Willpower/2 health levels vs. 20/2/2; Greater Storm -- 25/2/3 vs. 25/2/3; Gale -- 25/3/3 vs. 25/3/2; Greater Gale -- 30/4/3 vs. 25/3/3; Hurricane -- cannot vs. 30/4/3; Greater Hurricane -- cannot vs. 35/4/4; Tsunami -- cannot vs. 40/5/4; Greater Tsunami -- cannot vs. 45/5/5; Island Killer -- cannot vs. 50/6/6. A wielder who lacks sufficient motes or Willpower can convert health levels into motes or Willpower (one health level = 10 motes of Essence or 1 Willpower) for the purposes of paying the cost, but only if she also lacks resources to power the stone otherwise -- she cannot choose to prefer health levels just to leave herself with more motes afterward. The wielder can attempt to judge how strong an incoming storm will be with a Perception + Occult roll before trying to stop it; difficulty depends on the storm's intensity, how quickly it sprang up, and whether it has magical foundations (difficulty 2 to 5 for an extremely fast, powerful, unforeseen storm). A magically summoned or influenced storm is easier to predict and control: treat it as one severity level lower for cost purposes and reduce the judgment roll's difficulty by 2 (minimum 2). Lesser stones (green or light blue) can disperse most storms but do nothing against the strongest; a storm sapphire's power either works outright or fails outright, it does not partially succeed. Only the darkest blue and black stones can disperse any storm, at a life-force cost the wielder cannot know in advance. Creating a storm sapphire requires a flawless sapphire, the blood of a Storm Mother, and a wind spirit that has never before seen a mortal, captured alive; the enchantment takes a year and a day and must be performed on a ship floating in the clear waters of the uttermost West, out of sight of any land, which is why so few exist.
cost: Variable per the Storm Sapphire Effect Table (20-50 motes, 2-6 Willpower, and 2-6 unsoakable health levels, depending on storm severity and stone color)
compatibility: Any Essence-manipulating wielder able to pay the sapphire's cost in motes, Willpower, and health levels -- the source text names 'the Exalted, spirit or god-blooded' as those who wield it, and a raksha has all three currencies (Essence/mote pool, Willpower, and health levels) exactly as described (see fair-folk-creation-overview-common / -noble), so she qualifies without reinterpretation even though the text does not use the word 'raksha' by name.

name: Cord of Winds (Artifact •)
summary: A relatively common silken cord tied with knots, each binding a minor air elemental that will raise wind and serve for a day and a night if released -- notably producible by mortal sorcerers, not just the Exalted.
requirements: None stated beyond untying a knot to release its bound elemental (a knot-severing shortcut requires an extended Wits + Sail roll).
mechanics: A relatively common artifact, produced even by mortal sorcerers; partially depleted examples can be found on many ships, even relatively small ones, since they have been created in large numbers over the centuries. The cord of winds is normally a silken cord, usually light blue but possibly any color, adorned with a number of knots. Each knot holds a minor air elemental bound within it; if released, the elemental serves for a day and a night, raising wind when asked, and is free to depart once its service is up. Any attempt to detain the elemental past its term is poorly received and may bring retribution down on the offending party at some point. Most cords have 20 knots when first created, of differing sizes and complexities: the smaller, simpler knots hold elementals that are little more than breezes, while the larger, more complex knots hold more powerful elementals. Untying a knot in a hurry (rather than simply asking its elemental for service) is an extended Wits + Sail task whose difficulty depends on the power of the air elemental bound within -- a simple breeze's knot has difficulty 4, while securing a powerful zephyr or gale might be difficulty 10, though such potent knots are rarely bound into a cord of winds; most elementals or spirits bound this way have a permanent Essence of less than 4. Any knot can be untied given enough time, or simply cut in half if one is willing to destroy it.
compatibility: Any owner; the source text explicitly notes this artifact is 'produced by even mortal sorcerers,' making it one of the least Exalt-restricted items in this section -- a raksha (who has her own Glamour Sorcery framework, see glamour-sorcery-overview) or an ordinary mortal sorcerer-in-service-to-a-raksha could equally plausibly own or have made one, and simply untying a knot to call on its bound elemental requires no Essence or Charm at all.
notes: Chapter Four: Creatures, Gods, Charms and Artifacts, 'Artifacts of the Waves' section, 'Cord of Winds (Artifact •)', printed pp. 125-126 (PDF 126-127), transcribed directly from the rendered PDF pages (this book has no text layer). Found during the required cover-to-cover read of pp. 123-128, not in the task brief's own 'already-confirmed' list. No genuine incompatibility found; this is the single most permissively-worded artifact in the entire section, explicitly extending past the Exalted to mortal sorcerers, which if anything strengthens the case for raksha eligibility.

name: Wavecleaver Daiklaive (Artifact ••)
summary: An unusually short daiklaive, rarely exceeding three feet of blade, purpose-built for fighting in the cramped, low-ceilinged quarters belowdecks, with a thick curved edge that doubles as a tool capable of hacking through steel cables or chains in a single stroke.
requirements: Minimum Strength ••.
mechanics: Speed +3, Accuracy +2, Damage +5L, Defense +1, Minimum Strength ••. Wavecleavers are uncommon weapons, wielded mostly by Terrestrials of House V'neef and House Peleps, though most Dynastic houses have a small number of them. Perhaps the shortest of daiklaives, rarely exceeding three feet in blade length, wavecleavers are perfectly suited for work belowdecks, where cramped quarters and low ceilings are the norm. Their thick blades and strong edges make them as useful as tools as they are weapons; even steel cables or chains will rarely withstand more than a single hack from a wavecleaver's curved blade. Wavecleavers typically have sockets for two Hearthstones; Exalted who use a wavecleaver on the water are more likely to rely on those gem-like talismans for survival than on the blade alone.
compatibility: Any wielder able to meet the weapon's Minimum Strength •• requirement; the note that most current owners are Terrestrials of House V'neef and House Peleps is a setting/ownership fact about who currently holds them, not a mechanical restriction on who could wield one -- a raksha wearing a Mote with sufficient Strength could wield a wavecleaver exactly as any mortal or Exalted swordsman, purchased through the Artifact Background like any other two-dot weapon.

name: Light Implosion Bow (Artifact ••, ••• if Hearthstone or Reagent Powered)
summary: A First Age naval siege weapon resembling a ballista mounted on a heavy gimbaled pedestal, built of dark wine-red wood inlaid with the Five Magical Materials and adamant, that fires projectiles of pure Essence -- explicitly usable by any Exalted type, Fair Folk, and possibly others who can channel Essence.
requirements: A character capable of channeling Essence (characters unable to channel Essence cannot operate these artifacts); an unfamiliar operator's player must succeed at an Intelligence + Lore roll at difficulty 3 to decipher the controls before first use.
mechanics: These fearsome weapons are First Age relics whose workings remain beyond the full understanding of any savant or engineer of the present day, though their use is simple once the operator becomes familiar with their functioning. Resembling a ballista mounted atop a heavy gimbaled pedestal, the mechanism appears to be made of a dark, glossy, wine-red wood, with elaborate inlays and fittings of the Five Magical Materials and adamant (an incredibly strong, glossy material used during the First Age). When properly used by a character capable of channeling Essence -- any Exalted type, and also Fair Folk and possibly others -- the weapon launches projectiles of pure Essence; characters unable to channel Essence cannot operate it at all. It is fired using Archery, with +3 Accuracy, a rate of 1, and a range of 500. Before firing, the user selects the type of damage to inflict, and the amount depends on how many motes of Essence are channeled into the weapon: for 1 mote, the projectile inflicts either 7B or 5L damage (per the control settings) on everything within a 10-foot radius of its target -- in naval combat, this setting can be used against rigging, units, or troops. For 2 motes, range and area of effect stay the same but the damage settings increase to 15B or 12L. The weapon's pedestal must be secured to a solid surface to fire; it has an arc of fire covering 360 degrees horizontally and 90 degrees vertically (30 degrees below to 60 degrees above horizontal). Some versions are powered by hearthstones and some by alchemical reagents; typically, however, one of the Dragon-Blooded mans it and powers it with his own Essence. The weapon is not for the unlettered: a character must have Lore •••• and Occult •• to keep it properly tuned and charged. Maintenance normally costs Resources •••• every 100 firings, and fuel/reagents cost Resources ••• for 20 shots; these materials are difficult, though not impossible, to find outside the Realm and the largest Threshold cities. Artifact Ship Weapons table entry: Accuracy +3, Damage 7B/5L (1 mote) or 15B/12L (2 motes), Rate 1, Range 500, Naval Range Long, Naval Rate 3/turn, Minimum None, Artifact rating •• or ••• (depending on power source).
cost: 1 mote per shot for 7B/5L damage, or 2 motes per shot for 15B/12L damage
compatibility: Explicitly stated to include Fair Folk: the source text names 'any Exalted type and also Fair Folk and possibly others' as capable of channeling Essence into this weapon, making it the single most directly, explicitly Fair-Folk-compatible artifact transcribed in this pass -- no reinterpretation or judgment call is needed, since raksha are named in the source text itself. A raksha would still need the stated Lore •••• and Occult •• to maintain and charge it, exactly as any other operator.
notes: Chapter Four: Creatures, Gods, Charms and Artifacts, 'Artifacts of the Waves' section, 'Light Implosion Bow (Artifact ••, ••• if Hearthstone or Reagent Powered)', printed pp. 126-127 (PDF 127-128, plus its Artifact Ship Weapons table row on printed p. 127/PDF 128). The task brief's own paraphrase of this entry's dot rating ('Artifact ••• for a common version, •••• for a hearthstone or elemental powered version') does not match the header actually printed in the source ('Artifact ••, ••• if Hearthstone or Reagent Powered'); this row uses the rating and wording directly confirmed by visual reading of the rendered PDF page, not the task brief's paraphrase, and the stat table on printed p. 127 independently confirms 'Artifact •• or •••' for this weapon. STRONG FIT: this is the one artifact in the entire Fair Folk-relevant Savage Seas section whose own text explicitly names Fair Folk as eligible users, alongside 'any Exalted type ... and possibly others.'

name: Lightning Ballista (Artifact ••• for a Common Version, •••• for a Hearthstone or Elemental Powered Version)
summary: The primary heavy armament of larger First Age warships: a swivel-mounted siege weapon of brass and silver that fires a blast of lightning capable of burning flesh and wood to ash and melting steel or stone, powered by the firer's own Essence, a bound air elemental, or a Hearthstone of Fire or Air.
requirements: A character able to manipulate Essence to activate it (the weapon is powerless without an Essence-manipulating firer, whatever the power source); Lore •••• and Occult •••• to keep it properly charged and maintained; Archery Charms cannot enhance its operation.
mechanics: Lightning ballistae make up the primary heavy armament of larger First Age warships, with implosion bows and other weapons acting as secondary devices. Powerful, though shorter-ranged than some other First Age devices, lightning ballistae can damage even the heaviest First Age hulls, and the few still in service are carefully guarded. When fired, a lightning ballista releases a blast of lightning that sears and scorches whatever it hits, instantly burning wood and flesh to ash and melting steel or stone. They are heavy and complex, built largely of brass and silver, and require complex fuels and reagents in addition to an investiture of Essence to fire; a lightning ballista is typically fueled for up to 20 firings before requiring servicing and maintenance. Maintaining one is not for the unlettered: a character must have Lore •••• and Occult •••• to keep the weapon properly charged and maintained; maintenance normally costs Resources •••• every 100 firings, and fuel/reagents cost Resources ••• for 20 shots (difficult but not impossible to find outside the Realm and the largest Threshold cities). Lightning ballistae are commonly mounted centerline on the hull just aft of the prow, on a swivel mount allowing the muzzle to fire on a 270-degree arc, with 45 degrees of traverse (15 degrees down, 30 up). Only a small number of ships carried more than one, and few survive to the current day. Most were powered by the Exalted crew, but some were powered by captured (or willing) air elementals, or by a Hearthstone. A lightning ballista powered purely by Essence requires 3 motes per shot; one that binds an elemental uses 1 mote from the firer and 1 mote from the elemental; one powered by a Hearthstone requires a Hearthstone of Fire or Air rated above Manse •• to provide sufficient power. All lightning ballistae are designed so the firer must be able to manipulate Essence to activate them; the source text describes them as 'powerless in the hands of the unExalted.' Fired using the Archery Ability, though Archery Charms cannot be used to enhance its operation.
